title: How To Drench Your Students In Learning
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin critiques the common teacher habit of over-involvement in student work, arguing that pulling up a chair, offering unsolicited suggestions, and repeatedly checking in actually undermines deep learning. He describes on-task, engaged independent or group work as visible evidence that a lesson has succeeded, and warns that any interference pulls students out of the absorbed, focused state that produces genuine learning. He connects the practice of stepping back to the development of perseverance, arguing that extending independent work time without teacher input builds grit, concentration, and academic toughness that many students currently lack. Rather than disengaging, Linsin clarifies that teachers should remain intently observant during this time, taking note of strengths and struggles to inform future instruction. He closes with a vivid extended metaphor of learning as rain, urging teachers to model brilliantly, then recede into the background and let students become 'drenched' in the experience.
points: Frequent teacher involvement during independent or group work interrupts and weakens deep student learning.
On-task, engaged behavior during independent work is a sign that a lesson was effective.
Extending independent work time without teacher interference builds grit, perseverance, and concentration.
Stepping back doesn't mean disengaging — teachers should observe closely to inform future instruction.
The teacher's job is to model and inspire, then step off the stage and let students take ownership of learning.
quotes: One of the biggest mistakes teachers make is that they get too involved in student work.
In fact, once your students become absorbed in independent or group work, once they’re doing as you ask, it’s best to observe from a distance.
When your students are on task and engaged in the work you’ve given them, it’s a sign that deep learning is taking place.
One of the goals of effective teaching is to continually extend the amount of time your students work independently and without your input.
It means that you’ll take note of their strengths, weaknesses, and struggles in order to inform future instruction.
Set your students up for success, then step off the stage . Recede into the shadows.
